name: Nara Park
label: Nara Park deer
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/456314269: large area 'Nara Park' (5281 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Park with hundreds of free-roaming sacred deer.

text.description:
Nara Park is a large public park at the foot of Mount Wakakusa, in the city of Nara. It opened in 1880, which makes it one of the oldest parks in Japan. The park is officially about 502 hectares. Counting the grounds of Tōdai-ji, Kōfuku-ji, Kasuga Grand Shrine and the Nara National Museum around its edges, the area grows to about 660 hectares. That is far too much to cover in one photo, so think of it as a place for several small pictures rather than one big one.

The main draw is the more than 1,200 wild sika deer that roam freely among the lawns, pines, maples and cherry trees. Local folklore treats them as messengers of a god of Kasuga Grand Shrine, and today they are protected as natural monuments. That mix of grass, old trees and animals gives you easy, friendly subjects, with a hillside backdrop on clear days.

The deer are wild animals. Signs in the park ask visitors not to tease them, especially when feeding. Keep your phone hand steady and your snacks out of reach, and give the deer a little space. Let them come into your frame rather than chasing them. Take a few shots in each area you pass, with a deer in the foreground and a tree-lined path or the hill behind.
text.geographic_location: Nara Park lies in the city of Nara, at the foot of Mount Wakakusa. Tōdai-ji, Kōfuku-ji, Kasuga Grand Shrine and the Nara National Museum sit on its edge or within it.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Nara Park in the city of Nara, heading towards the foot of Mount Wakakusa, and check local transport options before you go. From there it is about 6 minutes on foot to the park, heading north. The phone icon on the map is about 400 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots of deer and paths. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for wide lawns and tall trees. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it for close-ups, so you can stay a comfortable distance from the animals.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 400 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Pause wherever the trees open out onto a lawn and take your pictures from there.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place a deer on one of the crossing points, with a path or tree line behind it. Crouch a little so you shoot at the animal's eye level. For a wider scene, use 0.5x and keep the horizon level, with trees framing the sides.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the deer to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright. Live Photos can catch a head turn or an ear flick. Portrait mode works well on a deer standing a short way off, as it softens the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter and the light is softer. Late afternoon can also be pleasant. On sunny middays, look for shade under the trees to avoid harsh contrast.

text.access_note: The park itself is a public park, but the temples, shrine and museum around it may have their own entry rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Tōdai-ji
label: Tōdai-ji
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1134669589: large area 'Tōdai-ji' (1369 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Great Buddha Hall housing the giant bronze Buddha.

text.description:
Tōdai-ji (the 'Eastern Great Temple') is a huge Buddhist temple complex in Nara, and its Great Buddha Hall (Daibutsuden) is the main hall of the complex. The hall houses the world's largest bronze statue of the Buddha Vairocana, known in Japan as Daibutsu. The temple was founded in 738 and opened in 752. The statue itself is about 16 m high, and 48 big lacquered pillars hold up the blue-tiled roof. The hall you see today dates from a rebuilding in 1709. It was strengthened with steel framing between 1974 and 1980, because the weight of the roof had put it at risk of collapse. The whole complex is part of the UNESCO listing 'Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara'.

The scale is what makes it photograph well. The broad roof, the dark timber and the wide approach give you strong lines and plenty of depth, even on a phone. The site covers a very large area, so walk around a little and try more than one angle. Keep the whole roofline in the frame, and have people walking through the picture to show how big it is. Check the official site before you go for current access, and for any rules about photographing inside.
text.geographic_location: Tōdai-ji lies in the city of Nara, Japan, and is one of the city's best-known temple complexes. It covers a very large area, so this view shows just one part of it.
text.directions_text: Use a map app to reach the temple area. The phone icon on the map is about 45 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full width of the big roof and the approach into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof ends, carved details and the colour of the pillars.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 45 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Take a few steps either way along your line of sight to clear other visitors from the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the horizontal roof lines level with them, so the building does not look tilted. Hold the phone steady and at chest height to keep verticals straight. Leave a little space around the roof so it does not feel cramped. Include a person or two for scale. If you can, take one wide shot and one closer shot of the roof or a detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright, so the roof tiles and timber keep their colour. Try a Live Photo if people are walking through the scene, and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day or later in the afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the frame. Check the official site for the opening times.

text.access_note: This is a working temple complex and a World Heritage Site, so some areas, including the Great Buddha Hall, may be ticketed or restricted. Check the official site before you go.

name: Kasuga-taisha
label: Kasuga-taisha
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1134481286: large area 'Kasuga-taisha' (1654 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Shrine famous for its thousands of stone and bronze lanterns.

text.description: Kasuga-taisha is the Shinto shrine of the Fujiwara family, founded in 768 and rebuilt many times since. In fact it has been rebuilt to the same plan every 20 years for over a thousand years, most recently in 2016. For a phone photographer, the appeal is the setting and the detail. The path to the shrine runs through a deer park where the deer roam freely and are seen as sacred messengers. It is lined with more than three thousand stone lanterns, and bronze lanterns hang inside. The buildings have sloping gabled roofs, decorative logs called katsuogi and forked roof ends called chigi, which are good subjects for close-up shots. The shrine and the nearby Kasugayama Primeval Forest are part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing "Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara", and the forest forms a green backdrop behind the buildings. Wisteria trees here bloom in late April and early May. The lanterns are lit only at the Setsubun Mantoro festival (3 February) and the Chugen Mantoro festival (14-15 August). From the phone icon on the map, the main subject is a short step to the north, so you can start shooting almost at once. Then walk on slowly, because the best pictures are usually the lantern-lined path, a deer in front of a lantern, and the red-and-white details of the halls.
text.geographic_location: Kasuga-taisha is in Nara, next to the Kasugayama Primeval Forest. The path to the shrine passes through a deer park. The Man'yo Botanical Garden is next to it.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the deer park in Nara and follow the lantern-lined path towards the shrine. The phone icon on the map is about 35 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gates, halls and lantern-lined path as the eye sees them. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in tight spots, such as under trees or in the cloisters. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof details and bronze lanterns, and to photograph deer without getting close.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From here the shrine area sits ahead of you, so you can take an opening shot and then walk closer for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use the path or a row of lanterns as a leading line towards the buildings. Keep the trees and lanterns at the edges to frame the shot. For detail shots, move closer or use the telephoto to fill the frame with a roof end or a hanging lantern. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines of the halls stay straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky or white walls look too bright under the dark trees. In portrait mode, shoot a deer with a lantern behind it. On the festival evenings, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a post or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late April to early May for the wisteria. 3 February or 14-15 August if you want the lanterns lit. Check the official site for festival times. Early morning usually gives softer light and fewer people.

text.access_note: This is a working Shinto shrine, so please be respectful, and check the official site for opening details before you go.

name: Kōfuku-ji
label: Kōfuku-ji pagoda
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '猿沢池' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '猿沢池' (way/59465653): middle (145 m across); moved 30 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/98093576: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Treasure Museum' (55 m across).
notes: Temple with a five-storey pagoda that is a symbol of Nara.

text.description:
Kōfuku-ji is a Buddhist temple in the middle of Nara, and its five-storey pagoda is the shape most people recognise from the city. The temple began in 669 and moved to its present site in 710, when Nara was built as the capital. Empress Kōmyō ordered the first pagoda in 730. The one you see today dates from 1426 and is a National Treasure, and the temple is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara World Heritage Site. The temple was damaged by fires and wars many times, and the Central Golden Hall was finished again in 2018.

The best-known photo is taken from across the water. From the south bank of 猿沢池 (Sarusawa Pond), the pagoda rises above willow trees and temple roofs, and on a still day it is reflected in the pond. The temple grounds themselves are a short walk to the north-east.

Before you go, check the current state of the pagoda, because some visitors have found it under restoration. Photography is not allowed inside the halls or the National Treasure Museum, so plan to shoot from outside. If the pond is busy, the Eastern Golden Hall gives a quieter view of the pagoda beside the hall, with trees and open sky.
text.geographic_location: Kōfuku-ji stands in the centre of Nara, on the east side of the old capital, just north-east of Sarusawa Pond. The pond and the temple grounds sit side by side, so you can photograph both in one short walk.
text.directions_text: From there the temple grounds and the National Treasure Museum lie to the north-east, about 4 minutes on foot. If you want the quieter Eastern Golden Hall view afterwards, it is within the same temple grounds. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the pagoda, its reflection and the willows together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the pond and the trees around it. Use the telephoto (2x-3x, or up to 5x on some phones) to bring the pagoda closer without moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 猿沢池 (south bank, the point directly across the pond from the pagoda). The five-storey pagoda reflected in the pond, with willow trees and the temple buildings around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep your phone level, so the pagoda and its reflection stay straight. Put the water line near the middle of the frame, and let a willow branch hang in at one edge if you like. For a variation, the Eastern Golden Hall shows the pagoda beside the hall with trees and open sky, away from the pond crowds.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pagoda to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the reflection stays dark and clear. Wait for the water to settle before you press the shutter. Live Photos can help here, because you can pick the stillest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Just before sunset, or early morning before tour groups arrive. The reflection works best when the water is still.

text.access_note: The temple grounds and the National Treasure Museum may have their own opening and ticket rules, and photography is not allowed inside the halls or the museum, so check the official site before you go.

name: Mount Wakakusa
label: Mount Wakakusa
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1427600061: the OpenStreetMap point 'Mt. Wakakusa'.
notes: Grassy hill with a panoramic view of Nara.

text.description:
Mount Wakakusa is the smooth, grassy hill that rises on the eastern edge of Nara Park. It is 342 metres high, and its name means "young grass". Its plain, rounded shape makes a calm backdrop to the park, and it is easy to fit into a phone frame.

The hill is best known for Yamayaki, the "mountain burning" festival. On the fourth Saturday of January the dead grass is set alight, and a fireworks display follows a ceremonial lighting by representatives of two temples, Tōdai-ji and Kōfuku-ji. The story goes that the custom began in 1760 from a boundary dispute between those temples, though other explanations exist. The burning can be seen from many places around northern Nara, and popular viewing areas include Nara Park near the five-storied pagoda of Kōfuku-ji.

For everyday photos, keep the hill's long slope as the main subject and add a path, trees or a few deer in the foreground to give a sense of scale. Wide, open frames suit it best. Note that the mountain itself is closed from 12 December to 17 March, so in winter you will be photographing it from below.
text.geographic_location: Mount Wakakusa sits to the east of Nara Park, in the city of Nara. It forms the grassy backdrop behind the park's eastern side.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Nara Park and head east towards the hill. From there, look north. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full slope with some foreground. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want the whole hillside, or use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the ridge line or, in January, the flames.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (top of the hill, reached by the signposted walking trails from Nara Park). Panoramic view over the Nara basin, with Nara City, Nara Park and Todai-ji's roofs below and surrounding mountains in the distance, often with deer on the grass in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon of the hill on the upper or lower third line. Include a path, tree branches or the edge of a lawn at the bottom of the frame so the slope has scale. For a wide, calm view, try panorama mode, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hill to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the grass keeps its colour. For the Yamayaki fire, lower the exposure further so the flames do not turn white, and hold the phone against a wall or railing. Night mode can blur moving flames, so check the result and try a Live Photo as well.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, when the green slope stands out against the sky. For the burning, plan for the fourth Saturday of January, and check the official festival information first for the start time, as the event can be postponed or cancelled.

text.access_note: The mountain is closed from 12 December to 17 March, and rules for climbing it may change, so check the official site before you go.

photo.artist: The original uploader was OhMyDeer at English Wikipedia.

name: Isui-en
label: Isui-en Garden
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/97082272: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Isuien Garden' (252 m across).
notes: Japanese garden with Todai-ji as borrowed scenery.

text.description: Isui-en is a Japanese garden in the old capital of Nara, and it is the only walking garden (a kaiyushiki teien) in the city. You follow a path around a pond, and the view changes at each turn. It is really two gardens joined together. The western part dates from the 1670s, when a wealthy tanner reworked the grounds. The larger eastern part was laid out in 1899. Each half has its own pagoda. The pond is shaped like the kanji for water, and two small islands carry a crane and a tortoise, which stand for long life. Stepping stones lead to the central island. The garden is known for its "borrowed landscape": the roof of Tōdai-ji's great southern gate and the hills of Wakakusa, Kasuga and Mikasa appear to belong to the garden itself. That is what makes it work for a phone. You can fill the frame with water, stone, trees and a distant roofline, with no fences in the way. Take a wide shot first to show the pond and its setting. Then move in on the pagoda, the stepping stones or the crane and tortoise islands. Walk slowly, as the best angles often appear a few steps after the obvious one. The garden also has a museum of traditional Japanese ceramics.
text.geographic_location: Isui-en is in the old capital of Nara, with Tōdai-ji's southern gate visible as borrowed scenery.
text.directions_text: Isui-en is in the old capital of Nara. Check the official site for how to get there and for the entrance before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole pond and the sweep of trees and sky. Use the default lens (1x) for most views, as it looks closest to what you see. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the pagoda, the stepping stones and the crane and tortoise islands.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front pond, standing on the garden path facing the Sanshutei tea house). The front pond framed by the Sanshutei tea house, with maples and reflections on the water when the leaves turn. Walk the path from here to find other angles on the pond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the pond's edge on a lower line, with trees and any distant rooftops in the upper third. Look for the borrowed landscape: a roofline or hill beyond the garden trees. Frame a stone, a branch or a lantern in the foreground to give depth. If you want a tighter picture, zoom in on one pagoda with the trees around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the brightest leaves to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky and reflections keep their colour. Hold the phone steady with both hands, or rest it on a rail or wall. A Live Photo can catch ripples on the pond. Use portrait mode only for close details such as a stone or a leaf.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light early or late in the day, or under thin cloud, tends to suit the pond and the trees. Midday sun can make strong contrasts under the leaves, so expose for the bright areas.

text.access_note: Isui-en is a managed garden and museum site, so entry may be ticketed or restricted: check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft light early or late in the day, or under thin cloud, tends to suit garden photography, and midday sun can create harsh contrast under trees.
The garden is likely to be a managed site with an entrance, so access rules may apply (not stated in the sources).

name: Nara National Museum
label: Nara Nat. Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Nara National Museum pond reflection (pond in front of the museum)' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Nara National Museum'.
notes: Museum of Buddhist art in a Meiji-era building.

text.description:
The Nara National Museum is one of Japan's leading art museums, best known for Buddhist art. Its original building was designed by Katayama Tōkuma and finished in 1894. It is built in the French Renaissance style, and the decorative stonework around the West Entrance is especially admired. It has been an Important Cultural Property since 1969. The cream-coloured walls, gold details and tall windows look quite unlike the temples and shrines nearby, which makes it a pleasant change in a day of Nara photos.

The best-known picture here is the reflection. A small pond in the forecourt gives you the facade doubled in the water, with green or autumn-red leaves around it. A photo guide suggests crouching low at the water's edge and looking back at the building. The same guide says autumn foliage may be the most attractive season. If you would rather have a plain, clean shot, stand back and take the whole building against the sky and the trees of Nara Park.

Outside, you can photograph the front of the building freely for your own use. Inside, photography is limited to certain galleries and flash is not allowed. The museum also stages a well-known annual exhibition of Shōsōin treasures in autumn, so the grounds may be busier then. Allow time to walk around the building as well as to stop at the pond, because the ornament on the old building rewards a closer look with the zoom.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Nara, near the Nara Park greenery. The pond is in front of the original Meiji-era building, but it is unnamed, so check the exact pond spot on the map.
text.directions_text: The museum is in Nara; check local transport details before you go. The phone icon on the map is about 190 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the reflection, because it lets you include plenty of water in the foreground. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view of the whole building. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved details and windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 190 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Crouch low so your phone is close to the water and look back at the facade, which is to the west. The photo shows the building reflected in the small pond, with water filling the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water's surface along the lower third line so the reflection and the building balance. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. For a different view, take a second shot of the cream-coloured main building with its gold details against the sky and the greenery of Nara Park.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale walls keep their detail. Wait for a moment when the water is still. Rippled water breaks up the reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Autumn, when the leaves are red, is recommended by a location-photo guide. Calm, still conditions give the cleanest reflection at any time of year.

text.access_note: The grounds and the outside of the building can be photographed for personal use, but the exhibitions are a museum visit, so check the official site before you go, especially for photography rules inside.
claims_not_in_sources: The museum is near the Nara Park greenery.
Still water gives the clearest reflection, while wind ripples spoil it.
The grounds may be busier during the autumn Shōsōin exhibition.
Pale building walls can lose detail in bright conditions, so lowering the exposure helps.

name: Yakushi-ji
label: Yakushi-ji
camera_source: Commons cluster (7 photos), weak. Moved 130 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 100 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/208682432: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Yakushiji Temple' (327 m across).
notes: Temple with an East Pagoda dating from 730.

text.description: Yakushi-ji is one of the most famous ancient Buddhist temples in Japan and was once one of the Seven Great Temples of Nanto. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage group "Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara". The temple was founded in the late 7th century and the present site dates from 730. It is named after Yakushi Nyorai, the Medicine Buddha. What makes it work for photos is the layout. The Golden Hall stands in the middle with a three-storey pagoda on each side, so the scene is balanced and tidy in a phone frame. The East Pagoda, completed in 730, is the only original 8th-century building here. It is 34 metres tall and looks as if it has six storeys, because small roofs sit between the three real floors. Most of the other buildings were lost to fire and rebuilt later: the main hall in 1976, the west tower in 1981 and the central gate in 1984. That gives you a mix of old timber and newer, brighter paintwork to compare. The East Pagoda was under repair, with scaffolding around it, until 2018, so check recent photos if you want a clear view of it. Take one wide shot to show the symmetry, then step closer for the stacked roofs and the tall spire on top. Keep the pagoda upright in the frame so the lines stay straight.
text.geographic_location: Yakushi-ji is in the city of Nara, in the area of the old capital where the ancient temples stand.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is given for this spot, so plan your own way from central Nara to Yakushi-ji. From there the middle of the temple is 104 m to the north, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene of hall and pagodas. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the pagoda roofs and the spire on top. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are very close, and keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Ōike (north of the temple, along the pond edge). Both pagodas and the Golden Hall reflected in the pond, with the hills behind. Walk a little closer if you want the pagoda larger in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use the centre line to show the symmetry of the hall with a pagoda each side. For a second shot, frame the East Pagoda alone and let its stacked roofs fill the picture. Include some foreground, such as a path or a tree branch, for depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pagoda to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks washed out. For the pagoda, shoot with the default lens (1x) or the telephoto rather than the ultra-wide, which stretches the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and warmer wood tones, and fewer people in the shot. Midday sun can flatten the roofs and make the sky bright.

text.access_note: This is a working Buddhist temple and a World Heritage site, so entry to some areas may be ticketed or restricted; check the official site before you go.

name: Nigatsu-dō
label: Nigatsu-dō
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Nigatsu-dō' (5 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/354993353: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Nigatsu Hall' (44 m across).
notes: Hillside hall with a wooden veranda and a view over Nara.

text.description: Nigatsu-dō is a wooden hall on the hillside of Mount Wakakusa, east of the Great Buddha Hall and part of the Tōdai-ji temple complex. Its front part juts out over the slope on tall timber columns, and the broad balcony along the front is the reason most visitors come with a phone in hand. From the balcony you look west across Nara's rooftops towards the mountains, with the large roof of the Great Buddha Hall (Daibutsuden) sitting in the foreground. The hall was founded in the 8th century and rebuilt in 1669 after a fire in 1667. The current building is a designated National Treasure. It is also known for the Shuni-e service, held every year since 760 and now running from 1 to 15 March. Late afternoon is the favourite time to visit, because the sun sets over the western sky behind the Great Buddha Hall roof. Stand on the main balcony and use the wooden pillars as a natural frame. Keep the horizon level using the gridlines, and take a few shots as the light changes, because the colour shifts quickly near sunset. Take care on the boards, which can be slippery after rain. The approach up the hill from the Great Buddha Hall is lined with stone lanterns and makes a pleasant, quieter photo on the way up or down.
text.geographic_location: Nigatsu-dō stands on the slope of Mount Wakakusa in eastern Nara, just east of the Great Buddha Hall within the Tōdai-ji complex.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop at this spot, so start from the Great Buddha Hall at Tōdai-ji and head east up the hillside. Guides describe a path to the right of the hall that takes about 5 to 10 minutes on foot and passes lantern-lined stone steps. Head to the Tōdai-ji area and the Great Buddha Hall first. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the rooftops and the Great Buddha Hall roof together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the pillars and the full width of the balcony in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x) to pick out the Great Buddha Hall roof or the distant mountains.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see Nara's rooftops and mountains, with the roof of the Great Buddha Hall in the foreground and the setting sun in the western sky behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Place yourself so one of the balcony pillars frames the left or right edge of the shot, and switch on gridlines to keep the horizon straight. Let the Great Buddha Hall roof anchor the foreground and leave the sky and mountains above it. For a quieter alternative, photograph the lantern-lined stone approach on the way up the hill.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sky or the bright part of the scene to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunset colours don't wash out. If the light fades, try night mode but rest your phone firmly on the railing, as a tripod may not be allowed.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon through to sunset, when the sun goes down behind the Great Buddha Hall. In early March the Shuni-e ceremony may bring crowds.

text.access_note: The hall is a part of the Tōdai-ji temple complex and a place of worship, so please be respectful, and check the official site before you go for current access arrangements.

name: Tōshōdai-ji
label: Tōshōdai-ji
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/218644927: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Toshodaiji temple' (426 m across).

text.description:
Tōshōdai-ji is a Buddhist temple of the Risshū sect in the city of Nara, in Nara Prefecture. It was founded in 759, during the Nara period, by the Chinese monk Jianzhen, who came from Tang dynasty China. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing "Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara". The main draw for a photograph is the Golden Hall (kondō). It is a single-storey building with a hipped tiled roof and a facade seven bays wide, and it is regarded as the model of the classical style. The Golden Hall is a National Treasure from the Nara period. So are the Lecture Hall, the Treasure House and the Sutra Storehouse, and the Korō was rebuilt in 1240.

The grounds are wide, about 426 m across on the map outline, so you can walk between several old buildings and take your time. The long, even roofline and the rhythm of the columns suit simple, calm compositions. Start with a wide view of a whole building. Then move closer and look for smaller shots, such as the tiles along the roof edge, the timber detail, or the gravel path leading towards a hall. Because the site is a Buddhist temple and a World Heritage Site, access to some buildings and the rules for photography indoors can vary, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Tōshōdai-ji is in the city of Nara, in Nara Prefecture. The temple grounds are large, and the middle of the site is the point shown on the map.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app to check the route to the temple. Search for Tōshōdai-ji, or the name in Japanese (唐招提寺), to find it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the Golden Hall as a whole. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and cannot fit the long facade in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof tiles, eaves and carved timber.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front of the hall, on the gravel courtyard facing the building). The hall's tiled, multi-tiered roof and raised platform, with the gravel courtyard as foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the roof ridge level with a horizontal line so the building does not look tilted. Stand back far enough to show the full width of the facade, with some gravel or sky around it. Then take a second photo at 2x or more of the roof edge and columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the roof or wall to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the tiles and timber keep their detail. Hold the phone with both hands and take a few frames, as the darker timber can blur in shade.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the timber and tiles, and the grounds are often calmer outside the middle of the day.

text.access_note: This is a temple and World Heritage site that may have entry rules and restricted areas, so check the official site before you go.

name: Heijō Palace
label: Heijō Palace
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/5654119556: the OpenStreetMap point 'Heijō Palace'.
notes: Reconstructed ancient imperial palace with Suzaku Gate.

text.description:
Heijō Palace was the imperial residence and administrative centre of Japan's capital, Heijō-kyō (today's Nara), for most of the Nara period. The capital was founded in 710. When it moved to Heian-kyō (Kyoto), the palace was abandoned. Over the centuries the buildings disappeared and the site became farmland, though the location was never forgotten. Excavations began in the 1970s, and large-scale reconstruction followed in the 2000s. The remains were listed by UNESCO in 1998 as part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara.

It photographs well because of its scale. The palace was a huge walled enclosure, and the open ground around the reconstructed buildings gives you plenty of sky and space. The Suzaku Gate, the largest and main gate of the twelve, was reconstructed in 1998. It measures about 10 by 25 by 22 metres and was probably two storeys high. It looks strong against a plain sky, and the wide ground in front of it was once used for ceremonies such as New Year celebrations. The First Great Hall was restored for the 2010 anniversary of the capital's founding.

For your photos, keep the horizon level and use the open space to show how big the site is. Then move closer for details such as roof lines, timber and tiles. People walking through the grounds help to show the scale. On the map, the palace point sits a short stroll from the phone icon on the map, so you can take a wide view first and then walk on for closer shots.
text.geographic_location: Heijō Palace lies at the north-central part of the old capital Heijō-kyō, which is today's Nara. The Suzaku Gate marked its southern entrance, facing the old main avenue.
text.directions_text: Head for Heijō Palace in Nara and aim for the phone icon on the map. Walk about 118 m to the south-east. The phone icon on the map is about 120 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the open grounds and big sky. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a natural view of a building or gate. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof details and carved timber.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 120 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the horizon on a lower third line so the sky and any building roofs have room. Use the open ground in front as a foreground. Keep the phone level so the gate and pillars stay straight. For people-free shots, wait for a gap in the walkers. Try a panorama for the full width of the grounds.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so a bright sky doesn't wash out the roofs and timber.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and longer shadows on the buildings. Midday sun can be harsh on the open ground.

text.access_note: The Suzaku Gate and East Palace Garden were opened to the public in 1998, but access to parts of this large archaeological site may vary, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, more flattering light than midday.
Other visitors may walk through the grounds and appear in photos.

name: Gangō-ji
label: Gangō-ji
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '極楽坊' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '極楽坊禅室・春日影向堂' (way/309678779): middle (35 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
notes: Old temple in the Naramachi district.

text.description: Gangō-ji is one of the oldest Buddhist temples in Japan and was once counted among the Seven Great Temples of Nara. In the Nara period it was about as large as Tōdai-ji, with grounds roughly 440 metres north to south. Most of it was lost after a fire in 1451, and the old town of Naramachi now covers much of the former precincts. Three small parts survive, each now a separate temple. The part best suited to this shot is Gokurakubō, whose main hall and Zen Room are National Treasures and part of the World Heritage listing 'Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara'. The hall was remodelled in the Kamakura period from the monks' living quarters. Its best feature for a phone camera is the roof. Darker tiles from the Asuka era sit among the grey Nara-period tiles, so the roofline looks patchy and layered. Stand in front of the hall and step back from the eaves so the whole roof fits in the frame. Keep the phone level, because the long, calm lines of the roof are what make the picture work. If you have time inside the grounds, the Zen Room is worth a second shot with the older architecture around it. The garden has moss-covered stone Buddhas and rows of jizo statues against the temple buildings. Photography rules can differ between the garden, the halls and the storehouse, so check the signs on the day.
text.geographic_location: Gangō-ji is in Naramachi, the old town area of Nara, south of Kōfuku-ji and Sarusawa-ike Pond. Gokurakubō is one of the three surviving parts of the old temple, within Naramachi.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Nara and head south of Kōfuku-ji and Sarusawa-ike Pond. Walk into Naramachi from the centre of Nara. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole roof. If you cannot step back far enough, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a close shot of the tile colours.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at 極楽坊 (front of the Gokurakubo hall, stepping back from the eaves to frame the roofline). The Gokurakubo main hall's roof, where darker Asuka-era tiles stand out among the grey Nara-period tiles. The temple is just to the south-east of you. Face the hall and step back from the eaves until the roofline is in view, with the darker Asuka-era tiles showing among the grey ones.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the ridge of the roof up with a horizontal line, so the roof does not look tilted. Leave a little sky above the ridge. Then zoom in for a second shot of the tile colours. For an alternative, photograph the Zen Room and its roof with the older buildings around it. You could also shoot the moss-covered stone Buddhas and jizo rows in the garden against the halls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the roof to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the tiles keep their colour against a bright sky. Hold the phone with both hands. Skip portrait mode here, since it can blur the roof edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even daylight shows the difference between the tile colours best. Harsh midday sun can wash them out.

text.access_note: The temple grounds, garden and halls are inside a ticketed precinct, and photography rules vary by area, so check the official site and the signs before you go.

text.description:
Sarusawa Pond is a calm, tree-lined pond in the middle of Nara, and it is one of the easiest places in the city to take a gentle, balanced photo. The main attraction is the five-storey Kofuku-ji pagoda, which rises above the willows and trees around the water. When the surface is still, the pagoda is reflected in the pond, and that reflection is the picture most visitors come for. The pond has a walking path around its edge, with wooden bridges and walkways, so you can try several angles in a few minutes without going far.

For something a little different from the usual view, follow the path and look for the pagoda seen through the trees. Foliage in the foreground makes the picture feel framed and quieter than a straight-on shot. The pond is busiest during cherry blossom and autumn foliage seasons, and an annual carp release on 16 April may also draw a crowd, so allow a little patience at the best spots. The pagoda and its steps lie on the pond's north side, while some visitors prefer the south side for the classic view. The angles differ, so walk a short way and check what you see on your screen before settling.

Keep your phone steady with both hands, use the gridlines to keep the pagoda upright, and look at the water for a clean reflection before you press the shutter.
text.geographic_location: Sarusawa Pond is in central Nara, just below the Kofuku-ji pagoda, which stands on the pond's north side.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Kofuku-ji area in central Nara, where the pagoda is easy to spot and the pond lies beside it. The phone icon on the map is at the pond. It marks a general shore position rather than an exact standing spot, so use it as a starting place and adjust along the shore. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the pagoda and the pond together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) on the bridges and walkways to take in more of the trees and water. If you want the pagoda alone through the foliage, try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) and keep your arms close to your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you can look at the pagoda through the trees around the pond, which gives a quieter, framed view. For the classic reflection of the five-storey pagoda in the still water, walk a little further along the shore. Views differ on which side is best, so check the angle on site.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the gridlines and place the pagoda off-centre, with a branch or leaves at the edge of the frame to add depth. Keep the horizon level, because the pond makes any tilt obvious. For the reflection, crouch slightly and include some water in the lower third of the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pagoda to focus, then slide the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the pagoda keeps its colour. Wait for a moment when the surface is calm before taking the shot. Live Photos can help you pick the best frame if ripples appear.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is a good time to be on the walkways and wooden bridges. Calm, quiet periods are best for reflections. Expect more people in cherry blossom and autumn foliage seasons.

text.access_note: This is an open public pond with a path around it; check the official site before you go in case of any local restrictions or events.

label: Shin-Yakushi-ji
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '新薬師寺' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).

notes: Quiet temple with a hall of twelve guardian statues.

text.description: Shin-Yakushi-ji is a Buddhist temple in Nara, just south of Nara Park, founded in 747 by Empress Kōmyō, who hoped for her husband Emperor Shōmu's recovery from an eye illness. It was once a very large temple complex. Today only the main hall (the Hondo) survives from the 8th century, which makes it one of the oldest wooden buildings in Japan. The other buildings on the site date from the Kamakura period. The hall is a National Treasure, with a broad hip-and-gable roof and whitewashed walls. Those clean lines against the tiles and the surrounding trees are what make it a good phone photo. The grounds are open and fairly compact, so you can try a few angles without walking far. Photography is not allowed inside the hall, so plan your pictures around the exterior and the grounds. For the main shot, stand in front of the hall and keep the whole roofline in the frame. Then walk towards the South Gate for a quieter picture. The gate is the oldest surviving example of its four-legged style, and it looks good with the approach path leading to it. Look too for the small belfry and the Jizō Hall, which suit close-up detail shots with the zoom. Check the official site before you go, in case access rules or entry requirements have changed.
text.geographic_location: Shin-Yakushi-ji lies in Nara, just south of Nara Park.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop right at this spot, so start from Nara Park and head south. The temple is about five minutes' walk south of Nara Park. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the front of the main hall. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you cannot step back far enough to fit the roof in. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for roof tiles, the belfry and other details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the 8th-century hall with its tiled roof and the open precincts around it fit in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the roof edge up with a horizontal line so the hall looks level. Leave a little space above the roof for sky and trees. For a quieter alternative, walk to the temple's south gate and photograph it with the approach path leading towards it, leaving out the hall's full facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white wall of the hall to focus. Then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the white walls keep their detail and the tiled roof does not turn grey. Do not use flash or try to photograph inside the hall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the white walls and tiles.

text.access_note: The grounds can be photographed from outside, but entering the main hall is separate and photography inside is prohibited, so check the official site before you go.

name: Saidai-ji
label: Saidai-ji
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '西大寺' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '西大寺' (way/211906944): middle (312 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/211906944: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline '西大寺' (313 m across).
notes: Large temple west of the city centre.

text.description:
Saidai-ji is a Buddhist temple in Nara, and it photographs best as a calm, open scene rather than a single landmark. Walk the grounds and look toward the Main Hall, the garden areas and the open courtyard. The temple is often quiet, so you can take your time over each frame without people filling the shot.

The temple was founded in 765 and was once counted among the Seven Great Temples of the ancient capital, Heijō-kyō. Fires and storms took many of its halls over the centuries. The monk Eison began restoring it in 1238. The Main Hall you see today is an Important Cultural Property and was rebuilt in 1808. The temple precincts have been a National Historic Site since 1965.

For photos, the temple grounds are the place to shoot. Photography inside the halls is generally restricted, and the interiors may be closed to visitors, so plan your pictures outdoors. Don't go looking for a pagoda to frame, because the old East Pagoda burned in 1502. Use the Main Hall, the plantings and the open courtyard space in front of it. Keep the horizon level using your phone's gridlines. If a few visitors wander through, wait a moment and they will usually pass. Mid-afternoon light suits the grounds well.
text.geographic_location: Saidai-ji is in the Saidaiji-Shiba neighbourhood of Nara city, in Nara Prefecture.
text.directions_text: Head for the Saidaiji-Shiba neighbourhood of Nara; the spot data lists no nearby station or tram stop, so check the route locally. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the Main Hall and courtyard. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the open grounds and sky. Use 2x or the telephoto lens to pick out roof details or a garden corner.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (temple grounds, shooting toward the main hall and the garden areas). The main hall, the gardens and the open temple courtyard, framed as a quiet, uncrowded scene. The middle of the temple lies to the north-west of you. From here you can shoot toward the main hall and the garden areas, with the open courtyard in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the Main Hall on one of the third lines, with courtyard space leading toward it. Keep the shot calm and uncluttered and wait for a gap if anyone walks through. Try one wide shot (0.5x), one default (1x) and one closer crop (2x) so you have options later.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the hall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and the ground keep their detail. Skip portrait mode for the buildings and use it only if you photograph a friend in the courtyard.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mid-afternoon, when the low sun gives mellow light and soft shadows across the grounds.

text.access_note: This is an active temple, and photography is generally allowed in the grounds but restricted inside the halls, so check the official site before you go for current access.
claims_not_in_sources: The temple grounds are generally quiet and lightly visited.
